utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. All the Defence teams. Mr. Krgovic is still working at home. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Vanderpuye. Ms. Frease is present in the courtroom. Good morning to you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You wanted to see a document yesterday, you asked to be shown a document that you were referred to during the cross-examination of Mr. Zivanovic, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have delivered these to the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Madam Registrar, have you consigned same to ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the witness has the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So shall we continue, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Yes, we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you wanted to ask anything on those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask for them, the witness did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we were trying to discuss, although it was late and doing it in a summary fashion, whether or not you found any inconsistencies with the various stories that you heard from the interviews conducted with the various operators. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then we talked about whether the logbooks were kept in the same manner in each and every site, meaning the northern and southern site. Do you feel that they were?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some differences between how they were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what those differences were?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And now I'll speak specifically about the military notebooks. The protocols or the fashion in which the conversations were kept between the northern and southern site for 2 Corps were very similar. But the way that the division kept its records were a little bit different. They were a little bit different in that they were more consistent in recording the date at the beginning of each day, and they also -- the operators very, very, very frequently signed their names at the bottom of each conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I can clarify, so are you saying that in both sites that they consistently did put the dates on or they did not put the dates on?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not at -- okay. At the northern and the southern site we had two units that belonged to 2 Corps, right. One unit at the southern site and one unit at the northern site. At the northern site we also had a division unit that was up there. That was the unit that I was just speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, about what the requirement to have signatures, did you reconcile why there was a difference between the various units as to whether they should sign or initial the intercept that they purportedly listened to after they made the entry?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about, did you ever discuss with various intercept operators whether or not they were permitted to analyse the intercepted conversation that they obtained?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by analyse it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, to make a determination as to whether or not the intercept was, as you said yesterday, important or relevant or to make a determination with respect to any of the contents of the purported intercept that they captured?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were given very clear instructions to write down only what they heard. So if they didn't hear a particular participant they would usually indicate dots, that was the most common way that they would do that, a sequence of dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two questions in there, I think. With respect to the contents of the intercept and you say analyse it, I -- I would say that -- I'm not sure how you're defining "analyse," but there were times when an operator believed that a conversation was very important, and in moments like that he would transcribe it quickly and it would be sent rapidly and sometimes on its own, where the other conversations would be transcribed usually within a couple of hours, and sent as a separate report of a number of conversations together.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about any evidence that you have taken from these witness with' respect to having purportedly a dossier or a profile of who the potential or some of the officers were from the VRS? Did you know if that ever existed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In which site?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the northern site.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if you ever were able to procure or find a copy of this dossier?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "dossier," I assume you mean a number of pieces of paper to put together as a compilation or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it could mean many different things to many people. During your interview process with these intercept operators, did it ever come up?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what did you ask them? What did they mean by dossier? How did they explain it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember them using the word "dossier."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What did they use?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's use the word chart then. Were you ever given a copy of the chart they purportedly used in the northern site?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for it but they weren't able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them verbally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know we talked about it verbally, I'm not sure whether it was in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How did they respond, in writing or verbally?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Verbally -- verbally, I think they said that they would look for it but it was a few years after the events, and they weren't sure exactly where those -- you know, that working document would have -- would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know what they said to you in connection with this chart, what was contained within it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it would have been the code-names of the various locations, and positions that some of the primary participants would have held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you which participants were included in this chart?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Informally -- or, well, even I think in some of the statements they were able to remember some of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That wasn't quite my question, if they remembered any other participants.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you which participants were included in the chart they claimed was in existence at the northern site?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they gave me an exhaustive list of who was included in the chart, is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking for an exhaustive list. Did they give you any indication as to who the participants were that they claim that were placed on that chart?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And some of them remembered, some of the participants. So they told me who the participants were that they remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you record that in any fashion, in any memo to file?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that information was included in witness statements and it's also possible that it was included in an information report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's just go back to your file. Did you maintain a file of all the memos that you prepared in connection with your duties and responsibilities as the head, if you will, of the intercept project?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a binder, my recollection is that I had a binder of material that I produced. I'd like to clarify. At a certain point I wasn't officially assigned -- well -- to the team anymore. So I wasn't sitting with the team anymore, I had other responsibilities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. And I understand that, Ms. Frease. What I'm trying to just get an idea of is, during the time you were not after you left or before you got there, during the time that you were there and when you were in charge of this intercept project, did you create various reports and/or memos to a file, and if so, how extensive was the file? Could you tell me, was it 20 pages, 100 pages, 1.000 pages?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that file would have consisted, I believe, of memos that pertained not only to the intercept project, but also to other work that I was doing, so other memos that I would have written with respect to other work. How many pages was it, I would say closer to, you know, 20 to 30 than 100 or 1.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you this: Did you find in any of the logbooks when you were reviewing them from time to time whether it seemed as if certain dates were written in certain sections of the logbook that didn't correspond with the actual handwriting of the purported intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you ever write a report to indicate in any of those logbooks on how many occasions that occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're here to tell us that the logbooks are reliable, am I correct then maybe a complete analysis would require you to, at the very least, from my opinion, respectfully, do an analysis, say, here are the shortcomings of this logbook or that logbook. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an ideal world, possibly. We were working with a large volume of material. Somewhere between, I would say, for the month of July, 1200 and 1800 conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's do it the way you did it. Let's do it through the methodology that you did called sample methodology. You're familiar with it, right, where you take a sample of a big group of documents and you make analysis based on that? Isn't that what you did, with some of the intercepts, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, well why couldn't you take one logbook out of the 191 logbooks that you had and use the same methodology that you apparently used in connection with some of the other testimony that you have given to give us an assessment as to whether we should rely on these logbooks by using the sample methodology to determine in how many instances in an example of a logbook were there where there were entries that seem to have been made after the intercept operators purportedly captured the conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would agree that they were necessarily made after, I mean, after what? I mean, what period of time? But the -- the number of times in my memory that that happened were very small, that the -- that there were differences in the handwriting of the -- the date compared to the handwriting of the person that was then recording that first conversation of the day. I would say that -- that those occasions happened very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you know, and why wouldn't you agree with me that they were made necessarily after, if you never made that type of analysis? Just because you've worked for the OTP? I mean that's fair, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've worked with the material for a long time and had an opportunity to go through many of the notebooks and a lot of the entries, so I think it's -- it's possible that we also asked the operators where we did have a question about the differences. If there was a date that was recorded by someone with a different handwriting, it's possible that we would have asked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I haven't seen that report yet and I'm sure we'll get it soon, but let me ask you this to change the subject a little bit, to make it easier, let's talk about voice recognition for a second. Do you know what it is? You've discussed it in some of your memos.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way that it was explained to me by the operators was that they had focused on particular areas for a period of time, and after having done this and from conversations where particular participants had identified themselves by name, that over a period of time they were able to then identify that person's voice when they heard it on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well let me ask you this. Did you actually, being a thorough person, as you were, did you ever do any cross check to verify or confirm, since part of your testimony in the last few weeks was to verify and confirm certain things, did you ever go back to verify and confirm if that individual operator who claimed he knew a voice of a particular participant actually ever heard the participant's voice prior to the date of the captured intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you just took his word for it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Why didn't you do a sample of, let's say, Mr. Beara, and his intercept that you properly corrected me on, it was the 15th of July, 1995, did you ever go back and say, Let me look if this operator ever captured any other conversation that could remotely be connected to Mr. Beara? Couldn't you have done that and then called it a sample methodology as you have with the other samples you have cited for us?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three operators, as we know, who captured that conversation, and if we would like to go back and look at some of those notebooks and intercept operators who captured those conversations, we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You didn't, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: What were some of the factors you asked the intercept operators when they said they recognised the voice of a person, did you list off for them what the characteristics are of voice identification and recognition?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what they are?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were there -- was there ever an instance where there were logbooks done in different parts, like having part one of a logbook, and part two of a logbook?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's say there's two logbooks.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find an instance where the logbook was identified, and let's hypothetically use the number 29, where 29, it was identified as being 29/I, and then a separate logbook being identified as 29/II?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do we have logbook 9 here? And while they're looking for that, if I could just put another question to her, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By always means, yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, it was my understanding from reading some of your supplemental information that my learned friend was kind enough to provide us that when they came to the site to obtain these logbooks there were hundreds of logbooks and then the process was that they selected only the ones they deemed pertinent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there, but yes. That's my -- yes. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But did anyone ever record how many hundreds of logbooks there were when they first arrived in the corps command, as you identified it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the sequence was that the -- that the notebooks were found at the northern site, that they had been moved there from a previous site, and had been under the control of the commander that was in charge of this process. That at the time, that was in March of 1998, when those notebooks were found the people from 2 Corps were surprised that they were there, and then a selection was made by members of the Office of the Prosecutor who were there at the time, based on the dates that were relevant to the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were they found in a cabinet, if you will?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if they were organised in the cabinet in any sequence at all?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean this is -- my -- the information that I have based on the information that -- based on information from members of the Office of the Prosecutor is that they were in a very disorganised fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor came the second time, were they in an organised fashion?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So even though the Prosecutor, after the first visit, informed them not to tamper or to even do anything with those documents, when they came back, they were quite surprised to see the same cabinet open, unlocked, and placed with logbooks in some kind of organised fashion, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander was quite embarrassed that they were in such a disorganised fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn from any intercept operators whether or not -- or was there a consistency between intercept operators as to how and to whom they turned over these logbooks to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was the consistency that you found?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is that when they completed the logbooks they would give them to their squad commander, and then when their shift changed they would give them to the commander that was responsible for -- for those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll compare that with the testimony we've heard. With the Court's permission, if the usher could assist us and place the logbook number 9 on the ELMO, and then we could return to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, while this is being done, could you confirm that when you use the word "logbook" it's the same as "notebook."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you like me to confirm that? I've been using it interchangeably, yes. I think it's one and the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, just to make sure that there is no one coming up later on and saying that "logbook" is not the same as "notebook." Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But, perhaps, Your Honour, we should -- may I ask the witness that so that we have her understanding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, of course. Of course. But you have been using the word "logbook" almost consistently, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought that's what some of the witnesses called it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, if I can ask you that, Mr. President's question, we have used the word logbook and notebook, do you find that to be a -- an interchangeable term?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use the term notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was -- were any of my questions, would they have changed if I used the term "notebook" instead of "logbook"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you were understanding when I said "logbook" that we're taking about the same thing, the notebook, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as an example we have number 9 on the ELMO in front of us and if we could just -- the left page -- no, the left page and just close the book completely. That's it. Right there. And that's what we're talking about when we say logbook/notebook, right, as an example?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now this -- I guess I will use notebook for the benefit ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Use whichever word you want. It's just to -- to avoid possible confusion by anyone later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that, there is the number 9 written on it, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that was written by someone at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either -- either at the OTP or the commander who was with a member of the OTP at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, right in the centre of that page, on the right-hand side off the centre there is some handwritten items there and I asked a couple of operators about that, and do you see underneath the RRU 1 that there is an indication that it's 29/II?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever inquire of any intercept operator or their supervisors or the captain what that meant?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the notebook and see what conversations are contained in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have a look, if the Court permits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Important thing, Mr. Ostojic, is that if you are going to refer the witness to it, the contents of that document, we need to know beforehand if it's the case of broadcasting or not broadcasting for reasons that you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Use your discretion and let us know, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having looked at it, it doesn't illuminate the -- my recollection at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So if -- what if I told you, and I think the representation is pretty clear by the testimony given by the witness, that the witness who testified on this notebook said that there should be a 29/I notebook?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that, if that's what he testified to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at notebook number 22, if we can. And we can remove number 9 from the ELMO for the time being. Are you familiar with this notebook?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we asked a couple witnesses about this notebook, do you see there where it's imprinted by the manufacturer, I think in Italian, the 1st of January, 2001?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On two different occasions, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever inquire as to what that meant?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know when the year of publication of this notebook was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever look on the back of the notebook to see if there was a bar code in order to determine when the book was actually manufactured?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever look in the back of the book to determine if there is a bar code to tell us when the book was placed on the market for retail sale?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the back of the book? Is there bar code information on the back of the book?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would that have been important, do you think, Ms. Frease, in making any determinations or formulating any opinions that you might have as to the reliability of a notebook to do just a little more than just do internal consistent reviews but to do a third party independent analysis of such notebooks, given that we have that information, and ask a forensic handwriting expert or some expert what the significance, if any, of both the date on the front of the book are, as well as the bar code information on the back?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We undertook a lot of checks on these notebooks, and had we had doubts and substantial doubts, had there been instances, I think, that, you know, had come up, a number of instances that would have cast doubt on the content of the notebook, the times that they were written, or things like that, it may have occurred to us, someone in the OTP, to -- to look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that was your threshold, if you personally or someone in the OTP had a substantial doubt, then you would go to the next step and ask a third party on an independent person to corroborate or to determine whether or not these are authentic or reliable, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many ways that we -- may I take this off so I can watch the transcript? Or are we still going to use this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We don't need it for the time being, but the Court ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Isn't it possible to watch the transcript at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because the ELMO takes up where the transcript is, takes up the screen where the transcript is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would it be helpful if I went through the -- all the various steps and stages that we went through in determining the authenticity and reliability of the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I've got your testimony on that. My question was specific: What was your threshold? Was it that you first had to determine there was substantial doubt before you took it upon yourself to hire or to retain an independent person to review the document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is substantial doubt a legal term?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, ma'am. You used it, and I'm just using it from your answer in my question so that you would be more comfortable.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just wasn't -- it wasn't something that -- that occurred to us, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did it occur to you to ask the intercept operators if they had made any changes, modifications or alterations on any particular purported captured conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean whether they lined through any of the -- in -- while they were transcribing the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be part of a change or a modification, but even more significant, if they changed, let's say, the name from a "B," which would indicate "Badem," to a name adding an "E," indicating possibly "Beara." Did you ever discuss that with any operator?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Which one?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about changes and modifications that were made to the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did that help in raising this threshold of substantial doubt that you speak of, to say maybe we should have a third party look at this? Did that assist in that analysis at all?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Why not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there wasn't anything inconsistent in what the operators told us and what we found in the notebooks. For example, there were some times maybe where a notebook didn't have a number at the beginning of the book. And the explanation was that, sometimes, there was a war going on, there was a shortage of notebooks, sometimes operators brought notebooks from their homes. When we looked at these conversations there -- there's a level of detail to the conversations that just further reinforced or didn't contradict the information that we were getting from the operators. I mean, there is a conversation, for example, on the 13th of July that we've talked about at 10.09 in the morning, involving Mr. -- Colonel Beara, and at the beginning of that conversation, I don't know if you noticed it, but it says he addresses the person that he is talking to as Sjor Lucic. The translation of that is "Signor Lucic." That would be consistent with someone like Colonel Beara who spent a lot of time on the Dalmatian coast. Signor, there are lots of -- as I'm sure you know, a lot of Italianisms incorporated into the Dalmatian language. You can say the word, for example, in Italian, which is "dirty," "sporco." In Dalmatian, it's "sporko." In the B/C/S language, it's "prljavo," which is a completely different word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, and that's fair, and I do agree with you. Did you ever ask any intercept operators that you interviewed, the less than ten or whatever it was, whether or not they distinctly remember that Mr. Beara had a different dialect, a dialect that comes from the Dalmatian coast?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't specifically ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did they -- anyone ever tell you that it was hard to understand Mr. Beara because he had a different accent from -- or a different dialect from that which we spoke in Bosnia proper, if you will?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to notebook number 9, if you will. I'm trying to just rush through this a little bit, and I know the translators have forewarned me and warned me last night to slow down, so I apologise to them again. I think that this is in evidence as P2319, and if we could turn to page 88 of that document. Do you see it? Yes. And if we can just kindly enlarge it, or at least the bottom portion, because that's the -- it's in e-court, actually. But either way would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need not to broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Now, if we could scroll counsel a little bit so we can capture the second half of the page. Yeah, right there is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't read it for a while, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know if there were any changes made to the first portion or the first page of this two-and-a-half-or-so page purported intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not sure. You mean these little -- like swirly scratch-outs and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is the nature of the objection. As to what my learned friend means by changes with respect to the document and specifically which change he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and I'll accept that I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- and will put a better question to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, I'm not interested, to be perfectly frank with you, about these little squirrelly changes that were made. I'm interested to know if you, as the person in charge of the intercept project actually examined this intercept to see if there were any significant or substantive modifications, changes, or alterations made to this intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In looking at it here right now, I would say that there don't appear to me to be any significant or substantive modifications or changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the word "riodite," [phoen] that's written above the X and Y on that page. Do you know if that was added at the same time that the conversation was captured by the same operator or at some different time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's written in a different colour ink, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, would that lead a reasonable person to conclude that it may not have been written at the same time by the same operator.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does it look like it's the same handwriting to you, just as a layperson?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to comment on -- on that because that is -- it's all printed, caps. [Court reporter leaves courtroom].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it, hold it. I don't know exactly what happened, but I saw our recorder leave the courtroom in a hurry, and, of course, the transcript stopped there. I'm investigating that to see what -- what actually -- of course, she may have a problem or something. Please, you will need to bear with us. We have a problem. We need to suspend the sitting, and then Mr. Ostojic, you need to go back -- was-- your question was not transcribed in full -- until we get a replacement or we see what's going to happen. She's not feeling well, so we need to stop the sitting for a while. --- Break taken at 9.43 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I said before, we had a problem which we have sorted out, and I wish to thank the replacement for having left the work that she was doing to come up to enable us to continue the sitting. I appreciate that. Thank you. We'll have a break at 10.30, just the same, because the accused haven't had one. So Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, before the brief interruption, I had asked you on the record, I think, whether or not right above on the exhibit that we're looking at, in notebook 9, P2319, whether the word "prioritet" was written above the X and Y, and you told us I think - I won't summarise it - but you started to tell us it was in a different ink or a different pen, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then I asked you, do you think it was the same operator who wrote it down, and I think you said you weren't able or would not like to give an assessment based on that or ...

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's just that the word "priority," "prioritet," is written in all capital letters, where the conversation is written more in a cursive style.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So given that you're not an expert, or I should say, not a handwriting forensic expert, that's why you can't really tell us whether that's the same person who wrote the word "prioritet" and the person who purportedly captured the conversation; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can flip to the second page of that document, which is page -- the back of page 43; is that the way we call it? Yes?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Something strange about that, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I think this was the notebook. I think we had talked about this before where I found we had gave these -- there should be -- if this is the notebook that this happened in, and I can't be totally sure, but there was one notebook that I mentioned where someone in the evidence unit had started to number the pages of the notebook. And I happened to see it -- this might not be the same one. Anyway, if it is the same one, then there should be a note to file by the person in the evidence unit who did that, who at the time didn't know that he shouldn't be numbering the pages of the notebook. So we could refer to it, maybe, by the Bates number 0077 --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will, but this is the same notebook that on the front has that -- of -- 29 Roman numeral II; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So we have some other problems with this notebook. Now, why did you not want this person or this fellow to write in the notebook the page numbers?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evidence unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because in original documents you don't want to make markings on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because then you alter the original state of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's -- looking at the second page of this document that we have on the ELMO - and I think we should have it also on e-court - looking at that, can you just tell us whether there were any -- and you used the word "material" yesterday or -- during your direct, the day before. Were there any material changes that were made to this part of the intercept that was captured?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I look at the notebook? Because I don't have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure. We have it on the ELMO so you may look at the notebook.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it on the ELMO -- or, I do have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just with respect to the word "material," can we -- are we attaching any weight to that word?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't my word.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Vanderpuye asked you that, he used the word and then you used it in your answers.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to be friendly and use your words, if I may, and you defined it for us, so just --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Any -- you asked whether there are any substantive changes to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I said "material differences"; I'm using exactly your words.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: See, what I'm trying to do, Ms. Frease, and it's not a secret, is to take your evidence and then to analyse it afterwards, and to try to establish what it may or may not say as a result of that evidence, so -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I see a -- you know, the letter B that was gone over a few times. We have a different page on the ELMO from what I'm looking at. I'm looking at 00779706 --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What we have on the ELMO is just the third page or the following aspect of that captured conversation. So I think it's the page prior; right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- actually, it's not. That's not what I have on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: E-court?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: E-court. I don't -- that's not what I have on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the e-court, for the record, we have a page which ends with the four digits, 9621.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. But that's a different conversation than --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would the counsel please repeat the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. 00779706, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, would you be kind enough to use, with the Court's permission, of course, and the usher's assistance, the pen in front of you and show us what you're referring to when you said the B was written over? But if we could do it on the e-court screen so that we could capture it maybe. Just circle it, if you will.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at this being the head of the intercept project, do you see any other material changes or differences in that portion of the intercept conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a little squiggle up above by the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just circle it.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- X. For what I see on the screen, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can scroll up a little. Oh, you cannot?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If we move the image, we have to start the markings again and we will lose all the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, and it was my fault, if we can maybe lose these -- I think we can remember what those markings are and she can make them on another one. If we can just enlarge it a little. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We did that on a previous occasion with other witnesses, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll just in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, if you could just remember those two markings that you've made. When the next screen comes up, if you would be kind enough and just re-mark those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise to the registry and the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A little further so we get the whole page. And perhaps because -- Ms. Frease, if I could just say, has the benefit of the original on the ELMO, she can then just compare the two and then look at the original and make the notation on the screen, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we do have the entire page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Frease, can you make those first two notations that you made, the little squiggly mark on the third line, and then -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to zoom out again, please, and -- no, that's zooming in. She will do it now. Okay. All right. So if you could mark again that little squiggle that you referred to before, and that B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I put the question to her?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any other material changes; and if so, please circle them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know how material this is. There -- whatever. Anyway, I'm correcting any little markings that are a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Whatever you correct we'll go through and ask you if it's material or not, perhaps. Just for the record, Ms. Frease, I thought you looked at the next page. I don't know if that next page is in front of you. So if you're done just with that page, bearing the last four digits, 9706, then we'll have them turn the page.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we also have the English translation of this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document right now has no English translation, unless you have another 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can't help you with that, Ms. Frease. Are you complete with the page, ERN number 9706? Any other changes or material differences or modifications or additions or alterations, or whichever word you'd like to use, on that particular page?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just for the sake of completion, I'm going to have you sign the document, with the Court's permission, of course, so that we could then capture it and date it, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, signature and date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On top of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Top right-hand corner, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then if we could get a -- or retain it, I don't know what the proper word would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we in agreement to scrap the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am, yes, because I think she's recaptured it on these two, and that's what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting is that we scrap it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a 65 ter number -- from the index of the intercepts, I have a 65 ter number for the translation. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah? 1164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you help us, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Before we go into the English, if I could just finish this little question on this document, Your Honour, for just completion, because there's another portion on the next page, just so we keep it all in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, Ms. Frease, if you don't mind. The conversation goes on to the next page, which is -- has the ERN number 9707; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it has page 44 on the top right-hand corner, which was added by someone from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it actually wasn't added by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Added by someone from the evidence unit?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just flipped through the notebook and saw at the end that it says that this -- it says in the B/C/S language that this book has 52 pages, and then it's signed by the commander of the VOD. I don't know what the translation for VOD is right now, the unit. And gives the signature of that person, who is the same person who wrote this conversation. [Check].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that this is not being broadcast, the page that we have on e-court at the moment. I confirm that it is not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On that last -- second page, page 44, with the ERN number 9707, do you see any material changes, differences?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you also, if I remember, did a -- basically a typewritten summary of each book, including certain information that you found on the front of the book or on the inside of the book, identifying each book -- notebook we're talking about, book 1, 2, 3, et cetera; right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have that material with you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On book number 9, which is the book we're talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you included in that on the front part of that book that this was part 2 of another book?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because this marking -- the reason that we numbered -- that the notebooks were numbered to begin with was that there was no way to distinguish one notebook from another. We couldn't say this is the book with the green dinosaur or this is the book with the chipmunk, because there were a lot of books like that. So, unfortunately, you know, you're not supposed to mark on original documents, but there -- for practical purposes, there just wasn't a way to do that otherwise. I think on the book 22 that you mentioned before, I think I noticed the number 4 in the top right corner, which may have been some number for them which didn't mean anything for us. I mean, we weren't able to put it in -- we weren't able to find an order to the books that were selected. So that's why these were numbered by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know who -- do you know which intercept operator actually wrote that on the front of the book?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever inquire?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it surprise you if I told you that was the same intercept operator who wrote what you just mentioned in the back of the book or on the last page of the book?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it surprise you it's the same intercept operator that testified here, whose statement you have taken?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that that intercept operator actually stated that that's an indication that there's another part or another book that goes along with this book, 29/I, if you will, Roman numeral I?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What efforts did you do to determine whether or not -- not only that it's possible, but that it was likely or probable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the thing is that we talked about this a little bit before, but the internal numbers that were used, assigned, by the 2 Corps were numbers that we didn't rely upon. They were their internal numbers. And to us they didn't -- they didn't -- they weren't really relevant to our processing of the books. I mentioned that at times we asked about the numbers to see whether they could help to orient us date-wise within the books, and essentially, you know, they weren't able to provide a really firm answer. They said, "Don't rely on those dates and numbers." So, you know, it's certainly possible that they -- that this operator, this supervisor, put this number on the front of the book and that he put that this was a second book to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you discuss with this operator or supervisor, however you want to call him, did you discuss any of the changes, material or not, that you found on that intercept that we were just discussing? Did you say, Hey, look, I notice that there are some squiggly marks or I notice that there was a change or material difference in your intercept. What can you say about that? Did you ever talk to him about that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think it would have been prudent to talk to him about it, if you noticed those material differences on the intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we were familiar with the notebooks and that the fact that the notebooks were working documents, and that-- I mean with the -- with -- for example, with the conversation that's still up on the screen, 00779707, there -- there's a line out, you know, through a word, through a couple of -- a couple of words. This was something very common, because as the operators listened to the conversation, if they listened to the conversation again, then they would make changes to it to better reflect the content of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can have on e-court the page prior to this, 9707, please -- I mean 9706. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you look there. It's my position, Ms. Frease, that the operator here added the letter E next to the capital letter B in the conversation that he couldn't hear from this purported "Be." Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, is it not possible, but it's likely, just based on your own observation of that document, that the E was added --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you talk to this supervisor or intercept operator as to how and why he made those changes to this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think that changing the identity of a person from what's been identified as B to something else by adding a small letter E, do you think changing the identity of a person is, in fact, a material difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do object to my learned friend's question. There is no indication that the identity of the person has been changed, although it is true that there is a difference between a B alone and a Be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. I think the witness can answer that question. I mean, she can tell us herself whether she -- in her opinion, the identity has been changed or not. And the question is: Do you see the material change, as is being suggested to you by Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You understand now why I stopped you, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, given that these are material changes, did you inquire from the operator why he made the change?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have -- I don't have a recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's just stick with this conversation for a couple minutes. There seems to be a reference to an extension there; do you see it? 155, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in the years that you've spent or the time you've spent working as the project manager, did you ever try to figure out whose extension 155 was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Some of the evidence here suggests that it was a man by the name of Tolimir. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the information that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's information from a witness that was here. Now, do you see in this conversation that this individual who was initially B, then became converted into Be, doesn't know whose extension 155 is? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be a reasonable interpretation; right? Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, where it says -- where the person who's designated as J says "155, that's up there, that -- higher house," or something like that, "call up there," you know, that's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to. It's the only real reference to it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's another reference before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. To Be or to who?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can just move along, in the interests of time. I think I understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we have notebook 99 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have it? We see it. Can you tell us what this information is on the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the radio equipment. There's a date. There's a number, 36, circled, and then over the pink elephant there's a number 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the date? Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that a 7 or a 5, the month?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like a 7 but it could also be a 5. There's -- it's, yeah, unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's unclear because it looks like someone may have written over it; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the 36 on the right-hand side, who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you inquire of anyone, as to who may have written it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, quickly, before our next break, when you did this written log sheet identifying each of the books, such as book 99, would you have recorded in that little reference to book 99 the information that's identified on the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could see the list that I produced, I could -- I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's more likely that I would have recorded the information that's contained inside the notebook. The strictly confidential number, 08/2/01/535, dated the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why is that? Why did you make that determination?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why? Because that's my memory of how -- of the information that -- that I was recording. I was trying to make a list of the documents that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, just open -- if you don't mind placing it on the ELMO and having us see the page that you just referenced. Does that anywhere on that page have the letters RRU on that page?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you your logbook, or your summary of each book, if you will, and maybe you could put that in the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this is really my only copy because we just recently received it. And I just circled it. I don't think it's inappropriate, but I would like my learned friend to look at it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, that's what I was going to suggest. You show it first to Mr. Vanderpuye and we'll see whether he has any objection. No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that, and this is just -- I'm just using your methodology as a sample methodology, if you look at book 99 there, which I circled, you include some information from the cover of the book and then in other parts you include other information from the inside of the book. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you include all the information in the front part of the book or none of the information? How do you make that distinction or how do you distinguish that? What I'm really getting at: What were you thinking when you did it and how did you do it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Ostojic. I produced this log a number of years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can have the log back. And then let me just -- maybe it's a good time for a break. I think I only have a few more minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. Let's have a break now, 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, we were looking at book 99 before the break. And I see you don't have it, but we'll get it to you. And the entry you made on your typewritten sheet summarising the logbook, I just had one more question on that. In your entry, and I'll get it to you if you need it, for book 99 --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we could just place that on the ELMO, the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On your entry for book 99, you have the following: "RRU-1/ICR 100 DR.08/2-01-535(14JUL95)." And you have other dates as well, but I don't think it's necessary for my question, just so the record's clear. You're welcome to look at this if you like. And now, what I'm asking you is, in the front of the book on page 99 that we see on the ELMO, although you've removed the book, is that -- the date on the front of that is the 16th of either May or July, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you have written from the front of the book the date as it appeared since you wrote in the information regarding the RRU-1, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 16th of July -- I'm going to call it a 7. I mean, it is possible that it could be a 5, but to me it looks more like a 7, so 16 July 1995. It says -- there are two letters before that say, "od," "from." In the -- briefly, when you showed me the list that I made, there are some dates after the numbers that were written inside -- the registration numbers that were written inside by the 2 Corps Command. They are reference numbers, right, they're strictly confidential numbers. And then after those numbers, if I recall correctly, there are some dates that are listed, and the first date that's listed is -- there are a sequence of dates. The 16th of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- right --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was the first one, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then there are a few other dates?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's a 19th, 21st, 23rd. Those are the only dates written in. Then after that it has the word "104 handwritten pages."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you're welcome to look at this to see if ...

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, the numbers -- the dates that were written after the numbers, and it would be helpful if I could have a copy of that to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the dates that were listed, you'll see in that list, are somewhat, I don't know, erratic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about arbitrary? Would that be?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say arbitrary --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Erratic.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because what they -- what I believe they reflect are the dates that were specifically covered within the notebooks, that were indicated within the notebooks. So, in some instances, you can see that there are -- you know, there's one day, then there's a span of time that's missing, and then there's a sequence of other dates that are there. And so the aim in producing this log was to record the dates that were indicated in the notebooks in order to help us process, to prioritise and process the notebooks in a uniform fashion so that we could, first of all, take -- well, first of all, we had produced a log, an Excel table, of the conversations that were -- that came through in the printouts, in those very rough first 550 pages we received. After we had produced that, then we set about cross-referencing the material that was in the notebooks with the printed material. And in order to do that, it seemed to me that the best way to do it was to make an inventory of all of the notebooks that we had and to record the dates that were contained within those notebooks. And in some cases you'll see on this log that there are -- not in very many cases, but in a few, there are references to specific conversations or names of participants who were talking in specific conversations, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It does. Would you be kind enough to place that document -- not that one, the -- your log, on the ELMO for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe the usher should be doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you look at this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First of all, if the witness would be kind enough to tell me what, that document, it is. She called it a log?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: She can answer, but we received the packet of information that's included in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- to identify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What this is, is a log. This is what I would call a log as opposed to the notebooks. And it's a -- I'll put it on the ELMO. It is a -- it records the basic information about each of the books. So the first ten pages, I believe, of this document go through book 1 -- it starts with book 1 and goes through book 134, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's enough -- sufficient. My question to you, Mr. Ostojic, is that -- whether we have that in our evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We just received -- we had just received it recently. I don't think we placed it in e-court because we just reviewed it, actually, last night, so -- but I think we could work through and get copies for everyone for that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that one of the documents that have been dug up now and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's my understanding. We got it recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And can I just confirm, Ms. Frease, that you created this document, is that correct? As a working document, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we saw the first page of that document. There's no title to it, no date or anything; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there anything more to this document, other than those ten pages that you've identified?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are an additional four pages that contain information about the additional notebooks that we received, so that starts at book 135 and goes through book 191.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is there anything in addition to that that would be in this material as log information, if I could call it that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a note to the file that I wrote on the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1999. So it would have been right after I received the additional 57 notebooks, or 55 plus the two diaries, on the 10th of May, I think, 10th of May. And then also the 14th of May there was another receipt which duplicated the material that was contained in that 10th of May receipt. And this short note to file - maybe I should put it on the ELMO - it indicates -- well, I don't know if we're publishing this, but there's a name in there that probably shouldn't be published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No broadcast, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it -- well, I don't know if I should read it or not. I can summarise it. But what it says essentially is that I received 57 notebooks on the 10th of May from this particular captain, and that I chronologically numbered each of the notebooks on its cover with a black permanent marker beginning with number 135 through 191, and that I placed my initials on the first notebook in this series, and that the first collection was handed over to me on the 24th of April, 1998, and those numbers, 1 through 134 were placed on the notebooks by the Office of the Prosecutor. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we proceed, transcript page 20, last line, line 25, always insist on the use of gender-neutral language here. But Judge Prost is indicated as Mr. Prost in the transcript, if someone could attend to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
