utterances.text: If we can just look at that, does this document relate to your logbook? I mean, is that -- what you did is have this memo to file on the logbook files that immediately -- or is it totally something separate?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be something separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because it doesn't seem to me that you had created this logbook, the 14 or so pages, until sometime after this memo; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, here it says two dates, it has on it, in the body of the memo or note, it says that you were handed over these documents on the 10th of May, and then on the second to last paragraph, it says, the 28th of April. Is that when they were numbered? Or when were they handed over? Or you're talking about the first and the second collection; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 24th of April is the second date, not the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. These were -- if you recall the first 134 plus 1, so 135, notebooks were handed over on the 24th of April, 1998, and those were the notebooks that were found by other members of the Office of the Prosecutor in March of 1998 that were then transported to 2 Corps headquarters. They were found at the first -- at the northern site. They were transported to 2 Corps headquarters and they were sealed in a box and then I picked them up on the 24th of April. Then the next year, in May of 1999, I picked up an additional 55 plus two notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we could just turn to the book number 99 that we were discussing, unless you have any other comments on that memo. Is my understanding of your testimony then correct that the indications after the "(14 July 1995)," those four dates you have there, the 16th July, 19th of July, 21st of July, 23rd of July, are the dates that are identified in the logbook? You don't have to go through it now, because we have the logbook in evidence, I think, so we could do that analysis. I'm asking you: Have you ever done that analysis, to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what -- yes, I mean, that was the purpose of doing this. And I would be happy to go through it now to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not -- I don't have that much time allotted to me, and the Court has been very generous to me. But my question, just briefly: Is it then true that there's nothing in that notebook that relates to the 17th and the 18th of July? Because there's no date on it, at least according to your notebook; right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the same for all the other entries that you made on this 14-page log sheet; right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I have on that, and we can move on to another topic ?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we could have P2319 on the e-court again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you that.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- what -- I mean, I'm -- you might have covered this with other witnesses, but sometimes it was possible, and I think we even discussed this, that sometimes it was possible to fill in dates if they went chronologically through the days. Sometimes that worked and sometimes it didn't, and if it didn't work, then we didn't consider a date to be firm. If it did work, then we did. And then it was further corroborated through the electronic printouts, the dates were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you ever make a memo or create a memo to file or to anyone explaining all that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that information -- I don't believe that I created a memo to the file specifically saying that. I believe that that was information that came through in witness testimony from the operators themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we could have page 88 of P2319. I'm sorry, I thought I had that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This is the same intercept we identified earlier, Ms. Frease, which talks about -- where it has the word "prioritet" on the front and you've identified it. This conversation, what -- in formulating your -- some of your opinions that you have here, what was the corroborating evidence that you had about this conversation? That it occurred and that it was reliable, as you say, or authentic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking whether there were, for example, documents or something like that that would have supported this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking you first: When you say "corroborate," what do you mean? I know you explained, you said documents, the VRS documents, then you said, I think, witnesses, then you used UNPROFOR for an example. For this particular intercept, did you analyse or come to a conclusion as to what the corroborative evidence is to support the authenticity or even the reliability of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you make that assessment or analysis for any conversations other than those that are in that three-ring book that you have, that you selected and called your sample methodology?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were additional ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, which ones?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who would know?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a folder at the time. It was, you know, in probably late 1999 or 2000. As -- as we went through the intercepts, we put certain -- I put certain conversations aside and then made a selection, tried to cover a lot of different sources in making the selection, which ones were to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you make a memo to file so that in case you left or were absent for a period of time, someone could follow your methodology, if you will, or logic, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have left the file, but I'm not sure -- I don't -- I didn't -- my memory is that I did not make a note to file with the other documents that would have been in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, there were some words in some of the intercepts that we've seen, and there's a -- contention as to what they may mean. When a word such as "triage" appears in an intercept, did you ask the operator what it meant?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. In your index, there's, I think, one dated the 16th of July. I might -- I think I'm right.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You use the word "triage." Did you know what it meant at the time, or did you not care what the intercept operator thought it meant?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in some of the conversations, participants spoke in euphemisms and your question to me was whether I know what triage means; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you ever ask any of the intercept operators what they thought it meant when they purportedly captured the conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about the word "parcel"? Did you ever ask an intercept operator that, what they thought that word meant while they were capturing the conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe this could help refresh your recollection. You took an interview, or participated in an interview, of a witness that testified here. This interview was taken on the 7th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if I can just go, for one second, to identify the witness, to her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the transcript, there should be an L after the A of his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that will be correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember having a conversation with that individual as to what the term "parcel" or "parcels" meant?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You said at some point you relied on witness statements. Would you have then not looked at these witnesses' statements in preparation for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first arrived in October, I scanned through some of the witnesses' testimony, but I did not study them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We can?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I hesitate to put this on the ELMO, but I'll make reference so we can find it, and it's in the witness' testimony. Because there's other names there, but if the Court wishes, I can place it and we just won't broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't wish, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You have no wishes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So I'll read it with you. This is your interview with this witness on the 7th of May 1999. Do you know that this was one of your first interviews with an intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time would seem -- the time seems right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because you yourself even said it was about a year after we received the material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So on the first intercept interviews that you did or was --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was I the primary interviewer or was I present during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You were present during the interview.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So it was a different investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dean Manning was the interviewer. It doesn't say -- and then there's the interpreter which we won't identify.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This witness states on ERN 00778117, second full paragraph: "I have heard references to 'parcels' many times on other calls and it could mean weapons, shells, ammunitions, tanks, or supplies of some sort. It was a sort of code word." Do you remember him sharing that information with you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did you follow up with other intercept operators to determine whether or not they had the same view as to what the word "parcels" meant?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you, when you interviewed this witness, have told that to anyone at the Office of the Prosecution what that word meant according to this witness?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine that I would have, but I don't have a -- I don't have a firm recollection of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean, you are putting the question as if she interviewed the witness when we have already agreed that was someone else who was interviewing the witness. She was merely present. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- if it was someone else interviewing the witness, why should it be --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- she to then draw the attention of the OTP or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what Dean Manning's role was in these interviews that he may have conducted of intercept operators?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an investigator and he was the primary person conducting the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was your role during these interviews of intercept operators?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to listen and to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But did you have a role at all, because you were the manager or one of the lead people on this intercept project, to make sure that all the information was captured and maintained and -- through one person?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there more to assist with, for example, the notebooks or the conversations that individual operators would have recorded, because I was more familiar with the -- with the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What role did Dean Manning have in the intercept project?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an investigator on the team and he, along with another investigator, were the primary people who were conducting the interviews, at least initially, of the intercept operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he work under you or were you subordinate to him?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, I was subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you remember what your first interview was of a witness when you came to the OTP? Do you remember that first time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object to the question on the grounds of relevance. I just don't see why it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. I mean, we do not exclude the possible relevance of this, but we'll gauge and assess properly, or more fully, as you go along. But how much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a few more minutes, Your Honour. I've shortened it quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the first interview that you took of a witness while working for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could offer a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- give us your best guess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, just a couple more items, just for clean-up. When I asked you the other day in connection with the exhumations how you weren't sure what your role was, and I should have probably on the two grave sites that I had for you, under Cerska and Pilici, I would like to just show you the third pages of those documents, even though they have some highlighted portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it's irrelevant, but if she could just identify that, that it's her name and that she participated in these two grave sites, for purposes that she's already testified to. And if the usher could just show it to counsel so that he can see the markings, obviously, on the paper. It's the third page, I believe. Yes, if we can just place one, the first one, with the front of the documents, just so we can identify which one it is. This one involves the Cerska grave site --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because Mr. Vanderpuye needs to confirm to us whether he has any objections or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would just -- and I believe I may have objected yesterday, and if I haven't, I do object on the grounds of relevance with respect to this particular line of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can respond, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's two-fold. I thought we covered it the last time. If Ms. Frease was involved in the collection of evidence, whether to establish chain of custody or to retain such evidence, there was a report, quite candidly, following her participation in those grave sites that we've identified as the San Antonio report, asking for certain recommendations and modifications to the practice and procedure that was utilised in connection with that collection and maintenance of evidence. So we just want to tie it up, because she seemed unclear when I reviewed her testimony, to the extent to which she participated in these grave sites, and that's why I'm putting it back, to clean up that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we have considered your objection in the light of previous questions and the explanation given by Mr. Ostojic right now. We do attach relevance to the question. So please go ahead and answer it, Ms. Frease, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, he may have objected before I finished the question. If you don't mind, I'll just put the question to her again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You see this document. It's the Cerska grave site; correct? It's a report by Mr. Haglund; right.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's a very extensive report, and I didn't bring the entire report, but at the back of the report he has a table of contents or index, reference sources, and I think in the last page of that document, references in two sections that you participated in the, what, transfer of evidence, under B and C? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. You were involved in that, as we called it, that exhumation called Cerska; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't involved in the exhumation. I think it's important to make a distinction between an exhumation and preliminary field missions and probing missions, if we want to call them that. I was present when the OTP investigative teams went out to the field initially in 1996 and when we were in the process of trying to locate and identify locations of detention and mass graves and other detention points, when people were coming down from the -- down from the hillsides. And so it was our purpose to try to identify these sites and to see whether further work needed to be done on them. I was certainly present at the Cerska site, the Cerska location, when we located the place -- when we located what appeared to be a mass grave. But I wasn't present, and I didn't participate in the exhumation process as such, which involved anthropologists and numerous other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we understand that. I'm not suggesting you were actually conducting the exhumations, and I used the term broadly, and I apologise to you. But what evidence, according to this, were you given -- or take -- what evidence did you take possession of from that grave site?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We produced -- I produced logs of material that we found at the sites during our first visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be the same -- or the same would be true for the Pilici site; correct? To short circuit it, why don't we just put the Pilici thing, even though this refers to both --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you do that, we still need for the record the reference number of this last document that you referred the witness to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but just before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you just said page 3 of that document, but we don't know which document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think earlier I said it was the last page but within my -- these were just my abbreviated notes on the document. This document has been introduced by the Office of the Prosecutor into evidence with Dr. Haglund, so the document is either in the Court's possession or will be next week. I just didn't think it would be necessary to duplicate the effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, this one is the Pilica; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pilica. And if you look at the last page of this three-page, very abbreviated section, document, I think your name appears on it; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And again it talks about, excuse me, the transfer of certain type of evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And this was done in those dates on that exhumation site or grave site; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be my preference to be able to reference my own documents rather than relying on somebody else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we asked for some or all of your documents. We haven't received that, but hopefully we will in the future. I think it's better to always refer to the witness' own documents. We can put that away. I just have a couple other questions. Do you know if anyone, including yourself, from the OTP participated in making the finalisation of the cause of death on any of the autopsies that were performed in these grave sites?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I reiterate my objection on the grounds of relevance. I think this goes well beyond the scope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this time -- at this time, you really need to explain the relevance of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think if we look at Dr. Haglund's reports, specifically in the conclusion section -- now I know I'm giving it away to the witness, but it specifically states who made the finalisation in both the cause and the manner of death and how it was actually done. And there's evidence, we think, through the San Antonio report that there was an issue, at least a dispute, as to how and what involvement the OTP should have in that entire process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we need to approach it in a different manner. You have sought to establish that Ms. Frease was involved, in one or more ways, in receiving material which was discovered in the course of exhumations or digging up of grave sites. I think before you -- we can allow you to put the question that you have put to her now, you need to ask her whether, after receiving this material, she was involved in the process of establishing the cause of death, as you put it. Because if she wasn't, then I don't see - we don't see - how your question can be put to her in the first place and how it can be relevant, at least as far as she's concerned. I do hope I've made myself clear, or at least I hope I have .

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you -- obviously, Ms. Frease, you heard Mr. President's question or comment. Do you need me to repeat it or -- did you understand it and can you provide an answer to us?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I understand the question to be is whether I received material which was discovered in the course of exhumations, or the digging up of grave sites. And I would like to make the distinction again between exhumations and the field investigations, the preliminary field investigations. I was involved in the latter and not the former. By "exhumation," I understand it to mean the formal -- formally taking material out of the ground, bodies out of the ground, in a very systematic way, by anthropologists and by other forensic people who are experienced and professional in this area. What I was involve -- I was not involved in that. What I was involved in was participating in site visits in -- early on to determine the locations of those graves that were then later exhumed. In the process of visiting those and identifying those locations, I was involved in cataloguing material that we located above -- mostly above the ground, as I think I mentioned before, like shell casings, like identification documents, ligatures, blindfolds, things -- things like that that we -- at dump sites and schools and places like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can just switch to another topic. I think we have our answer, and that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you had that list of names of various participants or officers in the VRS that you showed us during your direct examination; it was an index that I think is still in your folder of materials. Just asking you, in the brief moments I have, the name Ljubo, do you know if that's a full name or an abbreviated name for some other name?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is an abbreviated name for some different names. I don't know whether Ljubo by itself is a full first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have your index on the ELMO, if you don't mind helping us with that.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's okay. And then we're almost down, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We see the index of names, "intercepted communication." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fifth one down is a gentleman by the name of Major Ljubo Bojanovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not abbreviated; his full name; right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who created the document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was created with information from the military analysts, that the military analyst provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in what conversations do you believe that Ljubo Bojanovic was involved in, since you identify him as being on this intercepted communication index of names?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you gave me some time to go through the index of intercepted communication, I might be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have the right to any of that. It's at the Court's pleasure, obviously. Now, the abbreviated word for Ljubo would be what other kinds of names; do you know?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ljubisa, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the ones that come to mind right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In intercepted conversations where the name Ljubo was identified as being a participant, purportedly, what did you do to determine whether it was Ljubisa Beara or Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there is a conversation later -- a bit later in time that can be attributed to Ljubo Bojanovic because of the context in which it takes place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember who he may have had this conversation with? Like, let's say, Jokic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say that. Without finding the conversation, I can't. But -- no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think that's all I have, Ms. Frease, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. And I appreciate the extra time that the Court gave me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've been patient. Who is next? Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon or Bourgon, or whichever way you prefer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think I don't know myself anymore. Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a couple of issues I'd like to cover with you today, and I'll try to keep my questions as short as possible. I thought we could conclude your testimony today, but I'm not sure because I know that some of my colleagues want to ask you some questions also. I'll try to do as best as I can to be quick. First of all, you mentioned in response to a question by my colleague, and that was on the 27th of February, and that was on page 10, lines 18 to 24, the question was: "Were you aware of the possibility that these intercepts might have been fabricated, reinvented, corrected, and tampered with during that period of three years?" And your response was: "Not specifically during that period of three years, but that -- that was a possibility in general, yes." Can you confirm that this is what you meant, is that you are aware of that possibility of tampering and fabrication of intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were certainly aware, yes, very attentive, to that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I look at the -- having this possibility in mind and doing the work you had to do as the head of the intercept project, I would suggest to you that the best source that you have to confirm that a conversation is, indeed, authentic is the tape or the recording of that conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very good source, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, of course, it is a good source because on the tape you can hear voices and it would be much more difficult to fabricate or to tamper with, and you have time today to transcribe the contents and to really analyse it. So it is a better source, and it is actually the best source you have; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless the tape itself is fabricated, the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President; I couldn't agree more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a source, right, but I think other -- using other sources to corroborate the information is also very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question to you is simply: You say it's a source, you said it was a very good source, and I'm simply asking you to confirm reasons why this particular source would be good. And I suggest to you that, unlike the operators who had to listen to these conversations in a wartime scenario before they could transcribe them, and that they were under stress; if you have a tape yourself today it's easier because you have all the time in the world to listen to it and to transcribe it properly. Would that be another reason why recordings are better?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a reason why recordings are very good, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me -- you had a long conversation with my colleague over the word "material difference." My question, I'll try to make it a bit simpler. Would you agree with me that changing a few words in a conversation can alter the meaning of a conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would have to look at the conversations and the words that are different. In principle, yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, of course, if parts of a conversation cannot be heard on a tape, or, even better, if you only hear one of the two interlocutors or one of the two speakers, then of course that affects what you can draw -- the conclusions you can draw from a conversation; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another source that you use in this project, and I suggest to you that was your second best source, and that was the notebooks; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- second best source? I think they are very strong -- I think they are a very strong source.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would simply suggest that to you that on the basis that, because a notebook, if, of course, it's a true notebook, just like Mr. President said about the tape, if it is a notebook that existed at the time, of course it was compiled at the time the conversation took place, so it would be a more reliable source than something that is done after the conversation took place. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And another reason why the notebooks could be a good source is because those notebooks - and you've worked with those notebooks quite a bit - they illustrate the difficulties that were encountered by the intercept operators; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they certainly encounter challenges.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to these notebooks, I suggest to you that what you find in those notebooks - and to answer this question, I guess you'll have to refer to your knowledge of the interviews you've conducted with the intercept operators - I would suggest to you that they represent the best guess of the -- the best guess of the operators at the time; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the notebooks -- because there was a methodology behind the way that the operators recorded conversations that they heard into the notebook, and they were specifically instructed not to guess. And if they had any doubt, there are hundreds, if not thousands, of examples where particular parts of conversations or participants in a conversation or whatever are unclear and where the intercept operators indicated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm glad you mention a thousand. We'll get back to that number a little later. For now, I take it that you are aware that the operators, the intercept operators, when they did not understand parts of a conversation, the usual practice was for them to seek the assistance of one or more of their colleagues in trying to identify what was on the tape. Are you familiar with that, based on your interviews?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended. That didn't always happen; it did sometimes happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because we have, actually, many witnesses, intercept operators, who came here to testify before this Court, saying that it was a normal practice and that more often than not they had to listen, first, many times to the same intercept; and, second of all, that they had to refer to colleagues regularly to try and make up the -- to try and find out what was on the tape. So I just suggest to you that it was, indeed, a challenge for them in wartime conditions to try and come up with the real wording that was on those tapes.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's very difficult to make a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move on to a third source, I suggest a third source that you had was those printouts, and I suggest to you that the printouts that you received would be less reliable because, of course, they are computer-generated and everyone knows what can be done with a computer; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with the fact that a computer-generated printout is that, in the process, the easiest part that could be tampered with, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was the case, but that's very hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question is simple, that in between a recording, a notebook, and a printout, which of the three is most reliable and which are -- is less reliable in the sense of the possibility of altering the contents?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's a -- to me it's a very hypothetical question, and I think that, you know, some of the operators -- most of the operators really relied upon the notebooks and believed that they were a very solid representation of what they heard on the tapes. Sometimes I believe that the -- that the typist, that they may have listened to the conversations also with a typist, but the aim was always to transmit a very accurate transcription of the conversations that they listened to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, that's not exactly -- I thank you for your answer, but that's not exactly what the purpose of my question was. If there was a way to tamper with a -- one of those three sources, which of it would be more likely to be tampered with simply because of the nature of the material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it would be the electronic form, though that is not my experience with this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you also agree that, of course, the difference between a notebook and the computer-generated is that one is, I would say, some kind of a firsthand source, whereas the person who listened to the conversation and transcribed it, whereas the typing of the printout is secondhand and -- secondhand source in that there's a second person involved in the process; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a typist involved in the process, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it, Ms. Frease, that you were aware that there was no -- in the process, when the actual intercepts were taking place, that according to the witnesses that came before this Court, there was no supervision function. They would not -- once a conversation was transcribed and given to the -- for the electronic transmission, that there was no revision. Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My microphone is flashing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, I think it's a compound question. There are two questions involved in this particular proposition put by my learned colleague. And secondly, I don't think it accurately reflects the record with respect to the prior testimony that's been offered in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I have difficulty in proceeding, unless Mr. Vanderpuye -- Mr. Bourgon wishes to rephrase the question, I wouldn't -- if we are going to discuss this, I think it needs to be discussed in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do, please, take into account, especially the last part of Mr. Vanderpuye's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, I'll go -- I'll try to make it easier for you. Based on your interviews conducted with operators, was there any supervision exercise on the intercept-taking function, if you know?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would like to ask you to be more specific. I mean, yes, there were supervisors there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- because you conducted these interviews with intercept operators, did they tell you that once they had a conversation transcribed, that there was a second verification made by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think generally -- I think generally there wasn't, unless there was some uncertainty or unless the operator felt that they needed -- that they would benefit from having another operator listen to the conversation, to try to understand words that they were having a hard time capturing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll take that answer. Now, the -- in this case, I -- it is my understanding that you first obtained audiotapes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what is it that you obtained first?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We obtained the printouts and the notebooks and then later the audiotapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I quote you from an answer you gave on the 27th of February, and that was at page 18, lines 19 to 23, that "a mass of printed transcripts were transferred in January of 2001," something which you acknowledged when you were shown the actual document. Can you -- do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me specifically what those -- were those army documents or were those MUP police documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think you mentioned -- sorry, I don't want to overlap. What I'm interested, actually, is the 550-page binder. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 550-page binder was the first printed material that we received, and we received that in April of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in that binder, you mention that there were both MUP intercepts and military intercepts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mention that the intercepts done by the military had no headers.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And a question was put to you by my colleague, and I quote from page 21, lines 13 to 16, where you said that "in fact, we did not even know that there were headers at that time." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it that after some time you received those headers that go with the notebooks and the transcribed conversation, and that you must have spent lots of time trying to match the header, the printout, and the notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite correct for me, because we did spend a lot of time -- first we processed, as we discussed before, first we processed those 550 pages of printed material. But, as you know, there were -- there was material; there were sentences that were missing at the bottom and tops of pages because of the way that they were printed out and photocopies, and we've talked about that. And then from those 550 pages, and I believe those were about 1.200 conversations, then we took the notebooks and we undertook to cross-reference and to match up the printouts to the notebooks, to the conversations within the notebooks. So that required a database in -- so that we could cross-reference these -- all of these conversations one by one. And -- anyway. With respect to the headers, we received the electronic versions of the material. I received two diskettes which we were unable to open during the time that I worked for the Office of the Prosecutor. In December of 2000, I was made aware of the fact that the OTP obtained seven diskettes of the electronic material and that that was later - I don't remember the date - but later electronically stamped. Those were decoded and electronically stamped. And so it was then that it became clear that there were headers on the conversations. When I came back to assist with this part of the process, that was when I became familiar with the headers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And so you are able to confirm, then, that the headers is something that came in later, along with those floppies, initially those two and then the seven?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, for the military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd like to know if you are in a position to assist the Court in any way with -- why is it that the headers were only given to the Office of the Prosecutor later than the rest of the material? Do you know what happened with that material in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I know what happened with the electronic material, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With the headers. Why were the headers given later than the rest of the material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessarily that, I mean, that the headers were given later. It's that the electronic versions of the documents were given -- were given to us later. I mean, again even that's not quite accurate, because they were given to me in May of 1999, but the OTP and the information section here was unable to open those documents so we couldn't use them, so we couldn't see the headers. What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me try and make my question easier. You did receive initially intercepts without headers and then intercepts with headers.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I'm trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So not more complicated than that.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My second issue I'd like to cover with you today is the issue of the timing of the intercepts. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but the timing is something that would be very important, because if you have a wrong date, then of course it changes both reliability and what information you can draw from any intercepts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it also from your testimony and the material we have that dating the intercepts was one of the main components of your project.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And today, on page 24, lines 10 to 15, in response to a question asked by my colleague, you described in some -- in some way the way you went about to get the dates in the notebooks, and I'd like to go -- cover that process with you, so if you can confirm that process. So my understanding is that, first of all, you would take the dates that appear in the notebooks, those that are really -- that stand out, that are written in the notebooks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a step before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was taking the dates that were on -- that were contained within the binder of 550 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if you -- so you started first with the binder.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if there was no headers, there was no date.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But within the -- within that material, dates did appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As the contents of the conversations, you mean?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Above the beginning of the conversation. It wasn't consistent, but there were dates contained within those 550 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you ever compare these dates with the headers once you were able to look at them? Did you match the dates that you had previously with the dates that was on the headers once you got the headers?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next step after processing the 550 pages was to take the notebooks and to record the dates that were contained within the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again, correct me if I'm wrong, but very often there were gaps, and I think you used the word "erratic" in terms of mentioning dates in the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was true as -- that was particularly true for the two 2 Corps units, the one at the northern site and the one at the southern site. It was not as true for the notebooks that were written by members of that division located at the northern site and for the -- the police intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, just to -- a question that comes out from what you just mention, because of course you seem to make a clear difference in terms of the intercepts obtained from the northern site, southern site, and then the division. Now, once we have the intercepts in evidence, there's no way for the Trial Chamber to know where that comes from, unless it was covered by a witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that was just my question that arose from your answer. I move to my next question. If, in a notebook, you have two dates and a gap in between --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- my understanding is you tried to work things out using the sequence of intercepts based on time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You understand what I mean? So if you have, for example, one date is 10th of May and the next date is 15th of May, you would try to follow the dates to see when there was a change of date.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's what you mentioned to my colleague earlier, that sometimes that did not work.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when this did not work, then you went to secondary material, such as, for example, the printouts.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had pretty much already been through the printouts, so then -- if we had dates that were firm - I said this before, too - we bolded them; if we weren't sure about the dates, we didn't do that. We knew that the dates were extremely important. But then sometimes if a conversation was recorded multiple times - and I'm giving you, you know, kind of an example from -- or a hypothetical, kind of, from memory - but if a date of one of those conversations was considered to be firm and it was a conversation that was recorded multiple times, then we would -- I believe we would then consider that date to be firm for those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to -- let's try and take an example. I used earlier 10th of May and 15th of May and you have a gap, and then for some reason, using the timings of each conversation, it's not possible to establish the right date. If you then move to the electronic printout and you have a date and it says specifically "12th of May," did you consider that to be a firm date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I mentioned this question because I did this exercise with a number of notebooks and I came up with some questionable results that I have to share with you. Now, I can't do it with all the notebooks I've used, but let's use a few examples together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have on the e-court P1224B, for bravo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see it before we decide to broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could just clarify one thing with respect, again, to the electronic versions. We received those after I was gone, so I haven't viewed all of the electronic copies of the material that we received. Within the collection that we have -- that the Office of the Prosecutor is presenting, there -- yeah, I mean, the dates, with some exceptions which I tried to note within the date column, were consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't think we have the right one. I have one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I have a different one. 1224B.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. At the bottom of the page. On the right side of the screen, at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this intercept, that is a conversation between someone called Popovic and another person called Y, which is "who is unknown." Now, can you tell by looking at this intercept what the date is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No broadcast of this, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not without having access to the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, I agree with you. And it's not -- I'm not trying to do any -- I agree with you, it cannot be said by looking at this. So let's take a look, then, at the notebook, and that was in book 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would appreciate if I could have book 99 given to the witness, and that is -- for the court record, that is Exhibit P2330. But I'll try to use the original and I think it's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's put it on the ELMO, and again, no broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I refer you, Ms. Frease, to page 1468, that is, I mean, using the ERN number of the book, 99. Now, I take it you will agree with me that if you look at this page, which is 1468, that there is no -- you still cannot tell which date it is. I mean, the date is not specifically written for this intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Not on this page, no, there isn't a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we -- I ask you to actually try to establish the date using the sequence of intercepts and the timings of each conversation, I just have one preliminary question regarding the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let's go back -- if you can close the book and look at the first page and put that on the ELMO, please, the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this is the page that was shown to you by my colleague a few minutes ago, and you decided that it was -- to you, most likely, the date on the top left corner was 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you said that the words "od" meant "from" 16 July.
